title: How migrating birds navigate
context: Listen to part of a talk in a biology class.

lines.t: Every autumn, billions of birds migrate thousands of kilometers, and many of them return to the exact same nesting site the following spring. Today I want to look at how they navigate, because it turns out they use several different tools.

The first is the Sun. Birds can use the Sun's position as a compass. But the Sun moves across the sky during the day, so to use it accurately, a bird must also have an internal clock that tells it what time it is. Researchers demonstrated this by keeping birds indoors under artificial lighting that was shifted by several hours. When released, the birds flew off in the wrong direction, by an angle that matched the time shift.

Second, many birds that migrate at night use the stars. Experiments in planetariums showed that young birds learn which part of the sky rotates least, the area around the North Star, and use it to find north.
Third, and most mysterious, is the magnetic sense. Birds can detect Earth's magnetic field, which allows them to navigate even on cloudy nights when neither the Sun nor the stars are visible.
Having several systems is important, because each one can fail under certain conditions. The birds seem to cross-check them, and young birds in particular use one system to calibrate another.

Correct. The talk covers the Sun compass, the stars and the magnetic sense.

Correct. To use a moving Sun as a reference, the bird must know the time.
True, but that is not why the clock is needed for the Sun compass.

title: Why leaves change color
context: Listen to part of a talk in a botany class.

lines.t: Today we'll answer a question many of you have probably wondered about: why do leaves change color in the fall?

During spring and summer, leaves are green because they contain a lot of chlorophyll. Chlorophyll is the chemical that plants use to capture sunlight and make food. It's so plentiful that it hides other colors in the leaf.
But the leaves also contain yellow and orange chemicals, the same kind that give carrots their color. These are there all summer. We just can't see them.

In autumn, the days get shorter and the nights get cooler. The tree begins to prepare for winter, and it stops making new chlorophyll. As the green chlorophyll breaks down, the yellow and orange colors finally show through.

Red is a little different. Red colors are not already in the leaf. Some trees, like many maples, actually produce red chemicals in autumn. Sunny days and cool nights help them make more of it. That's why the fall colors are especially bright in some years.
So the best autumn colors usually come after a season with lots of sunny days and cool, but not freezing, nights.

Correct. The talk explains where yellow, orange and red autumn colors come from.

title: The slow acceptance of continental drift
context: Listen to part of a talk in a history of science class.

lines.t: When Alfred Wegener proposed in nineteen twelve that the continents had once been joined and had since drifted apart, his evidence was, in hindsight, quite persuasive. The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together remarkably well, and identical fossils of land reptiles turned up on continents now separated by vast oceans.
Yet for roughly half a century, most geologists rejected the idea, some with open hostility. Why?

It's tempting to see this as simple conservatism, but that would be unfair. The central objection was mechanism. Wegener couldn't explain what force could push continents through the solid ocean floor, and physicists calculated that the forces he did propose were far too weak. To many scientists, accepting an effect without any plausible cause seemed less like boldness than carelessness.

What eventually changed minds wasn't a better argument about fossils. It was new data from the ocean floor itself. In the nineteen fifties and sixties, surveys revealed that the sea floor was spreading outward from mid-ocean ridges, with magnetic stripes in the rock recording that process. This supplied the missing mechanism: continents aren't plowing through the ocean floor; they're carried along with it.
The episode is often told as the story of a lone genius ignored. I'd suggest it's better read as an illustration of how science weighs evidence of a pattern against an explanation of its cause.

Correct. The talk explains the initial rejection and the evidence that later changed minds.

title: The bystander effect
context: Listen to part of a talk in a psychology class.

lines.t: Today we're looking at a well-known idea in social psychology called the bystander effect. It refers to the finding that people are less likely to help someone in an emergency when other people are present.

In a classic experiment, students were placed in separate rooms and talked with each other over an intercom. During the conversation, one participant, who was actually working with the researchers, appeared to have a medical emergency. When participants believed they were the only other person listening, most of them went for help quickly. When they believed four other people were also listening, far fewer helped, and those who did took longer.

Researchers proposed two main explanations. The first is diffusion of responsibility. When many people are present, each person feels less personally responsible, since someone else could act. The second is social influence. In an unclear situation, we look at others to decide whether something is really an emergency. If everyone else looks calm, we may conclude that nothing is wrong, even though they're all doing the same thing we are.

There's a practical lesson here. If you ever need help in a crowd, don't call out to everyone. Point to one specific person and tell them directly what to do, like, you in the blue jacket, call an ambulance.

Correct. The talk defines and explains the bystander effect.

questions.explanation: The professor presents the bystander effect, a classic experiment and two explanations.

questions.evidence: we look at others to decide whether something is really an emergency

Correct. Naming one person counters diffusion of responsibility.

title: The phases of the Moon
context: Listen to part of a talk in an astronomy class.

lines.t: Today we're going to talk about the phases of the Moon. Many people think the Moon changes shape because the Earth's shadow covers part of it. That's a very common mistake.
The Moon doesn't make its own light. We see it because it reflects light from the Sun. At any time, half of the Moon is lit by the Sun, and the other half is dark.

As the Moon travels around the Earth, which takes about a month, we see different amounts of that lit half. When the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun, the lit side faces away from us, and we can hardly see the Moon at all. This is called a new moon.

About two weeks later, the Moon is on the other side of the Earth. Now the whole lit side faces us, and we see a full moon. In between, we see a crescent or a half moon, depending on the Moon's position.
So what about the Earth's shadow? It does fall on the Moon sometimes, but that is a different event, called a lunar eclipse. It only happens occasionally, and only during a full moon.

Correct. The talk explains the real cause of the Moon's phases.
The Sun's light production is not explained.

title: Linguistic relativity revisited
context: Listen to part of a talk in a linguistics class.

lines.t: Today I want to revisit linguistic relativity, the proposal that the language we speak shapes how we think. In its strongest form, sometimes called linguistic determinism, the claim is that language actually limits thought, so that speakers simply can't conceive of distinctions their language doesn't encode. That strong version has very little support. If it were true, translation would be impossible, and so would learning a concept for which you don't yet have a word.

The weaker version, that language nudges attention and memory in particular directions, has fared considerably better. Consider spatial reference. English speakers typically describe space relative to the body: the cup is to my left. But speakers of some Indigenous Australian languages, such as Guugu Yimithirr, use compass directions even for small arrangements: the cup is to the north.

In experiments, speakers were shown objects arranged on a table, then turned around to face the opposite direction and asked to recreate the arrangement. English speakers tended to preserve left and right relative to themselves, whereas Guugu Yimithirr speakers preserved the compass orientation.
But couldn't that just reflect culture, rather than language itself?

That's precisely the difficulty. Language and culture are deeply intertwined, so it's hard to isolate one as the cause. What the findings do establish is that habitual ways of speaking go hand in hand with habitual ways of attending to the world.

questions.explanation: The professor contrasts strong and weak linguistic relativity and evaluates the evidence for each.

questions.evidence: If it were true, translation would be impossible
